transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2025-12-22 15:42 UTC
- Duration: ~54 minutes
- Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Kestrel Eng Lead), Maya Ortiz (Platform), Samir Rao (SecOps), Lina Park (DevEx)

Summary: quick hands-on pairing to get Kestrel’s devs into the Redwood sandbox, walk through the Python and TypeScript SDK quickstarts, set up auth/CI secrets, and outline pilot success metrics. Short demo of Redwood Console & Optimize suggestions for batching.

Topics: SDK quickstart (py/ts), auth patterns (API keys, SSO), sandbox envs, CI secrets, console routes, Optimize batching/caching, data residency / SOC2 questions.

[00:00] Alex (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for carving time, should be about 45–60 minutes; quick pairing session to get you into the sandbox, run the quickstart and show the console.
[00:18] Jordan (Kestrel): Sounds good, we’re mostly focused on getting devs unblocked today, and then we want to run a small pilot to validate latency vs cost for our summarization feature.
[00:26] Priya (Redwood): Great — quick intro from me, I’ll walk the SDK snippets and common CI patterns, also show how Redwood Optimize suggests batching and caching configs for your workload.
[00:35] Maya (Kestrel): We’ll want to pair on auth — our infra team prefers not to put keys into developers’ local files, we use Vault and hashed secrets in CI.

[01:05] Alex: Totally — in the sandbox we can show both patterns: local env var for dev and a CI snippet that reads from Hashi, or you can use the private deployment keystore for on-prem. There’s a short caveat: sandbox keys are time-limited and flagged for PII etc.
[01:30] Samir (Kestrel): When you say private deployment, do you mean the Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem) option? Is that the only way to get KMS/HSM integration?
[01:45] Priya: Short answer: you can integrate KMS with both Dedicated and Private. Hosted also supports envelope-encryption with customer-managed keys for some enterprise tiers, but full HSM-backed workflows are usually Private. We’ll send the KMS integration doc after.
[02:10] Jordan: Cool — also latency: our 95th percentile must be under 350ms for short chats (<=128 tokens). How does batching affect that?
[02:24] Priya: Good question — batching improves throughput but can add head-of-line latency; Redwood Optimize suggests per-route batching profiles. For chat-like short requests we recommend continuous batching with small max batch sizes and an adaptive wait threshold — you get cost savings without pushing 95p over your SLO. We’ll run a simulated workload in the pilot to pick numbers.

[03:15] Alex: Ok let’s pivot to the quickstart — I’m going to post the repo link in chat: https://redwood.place/sandbox/quickstart (note: placeholder link). I’ll walk the Python example first.
[03:30] Speaker 1: (typing noises)
[03:38] Priya: In Python we show installing redwood-sdk, setting REDWOOD_API_KEY as an env var, and a tiny snippet that calls client.generate(...). A common gotcha is forgetting to pin the model or the tokenization changes which can alter cost.
[03:58] Lina (Kestrel): Sorry quick Q — do you provide a typed client for TypeScript? Our front end team wants TS types.
[04:08] Priya: Yes, we publish @redwood/sdk with strong TS types; the quickstart repo has both a Node example and a browser-ish example that uses a server-side token exchange. We avoid shipping keys to the browser.
[04:28] Jordan: Can you show the CI pattern you mentioned? We use GitHub Actions and need an example for secrets and PR checks.
[04:35] Priya: Sure. In the repo there’s .github/workflows/ci.yml: it reads REDWOOD_API_KEY from repo secrets, runs unit tests that stub the client (we include a mock harness), and for integration tests we show a separate job that hits the sandbox with a limited key. We recommend an allowlist for IPs if you run integration jobs that call the hosted API.

[05:50] Alex: I’ll demo the console now — short screen share but I’ll narrate. The Console shows per-route latency/cost, token breakdown, and Optimize suggestions. You can pin model versions and configure rollout policies (canary, A/B).
[06:20] Maya: On region/data residency, we operate EU-only for regulated customers; can Redwood host sandbox in eu-west or do we need a Private deployment?
[06:35] Priya: Hosted supports region pinning for production in certain tiers; for strict data residency we usually recommend Private or Dedicated with VPC. Sandbox can be spun up in eu-west for trials if you want. We’ll note that in the next steps.

[07:12] Samir: Security check — audit logs, SSO (SAML), RBAC? We need to show to InfoSec.
[07:20] Alex: Yep — we have RBAC in the Console, SAML/SSO via SSO provider, and detailed audit logs with timestamps and token-level metadata. Priya will drop our SOC2 summary and the audit log sample.
[07:40] Priya: Quick nit: sometimes the transcript beats me on acronyms — SAML sometimes becomes 'samm-el' in the transcripts.

[08:05] Priya: Back to SDK — showing a live snippet: (reads) from redwood import RedwoodClient; client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY'))... then client.chat.create(messages=...). For TS: const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); await client.chat.create({ messages });
[08:44] Jordan: Are there official codegen or typed prompts for structured outputs? We need JSON outputs consistently parsed.
[08:55] Priya: We support function-calling style and structured output helpers — the SDK returns parsed JSON in many of the examples, but you can also use schema validators. Also Redwood Optimize will surface when structured outputs start drifting and suggest a model or temperature change.

[10:10] Alex: Let’s run the quick local demo — I’ll hand control to Jordan and Lina to run the repo tests.
[10:21] (button clicks, a short pause)
[11:02] Jordan: Ok I pulled the repo, installed deps. The Python test fails with a 401, suspect the env var wasn’t set.
[11:15] Alex: That’s expected — I’ll paste a temporary sandbox key in the chat; remember these keys are short-lived and only for dev.
[11:28] Speaker 2: (key pasted) "--sandbox-key-hidden--"
[11:40] Jordan: Tests passing now, cool. The TS example needed a small tweak (tsconfig target) but otherwise fine.
[12:05] Maya: About cost: our batch job will call embedding endpoints a lot — any guidance for embeddings and caching?
[12:18] Priya: For embeddings we recommend caching at the vector store layer (Redis or Faiss) and deduping requests. For high-throughput you can use Redwood Optimize to recommend quantized model variants and batch sizes; for embeddings there's an unused tokens optimization that can drop cost by ~25% in our internal benchmarks.

[13:04] Jordan: We might need dedicated capacity if throughput is high — is it easy to lift-and-shift from hosted to Dedicated?
[13:16] Alex: Yes, the API and routes are consistent so you can point the same client config to a Dedicated endpoint and keep the same SDK. You can also pin model versions to avoid surprises during the move.

[14:00] Samir: A couple SecOps items: does the audit log include full request/response or just metadata? Also data retention policies?
[14:12] Priya: We log metadata and token counts by default; request/response can be included under enterprise audit logging with appropriate controls. Retention is configurable; common pattern is short-term full logs and long-term metadata-only. We have SOC2 docs that outline retention and redaction rules.

[15:00] Alex: Quick note about the Optimize panel in the Console — it surfaces batching candidates and KV (kay-vee) cache hits; it will show per-route unit economics. You can run a simulated run and get a suggested quantization profile.
[15:25] Lina: Nice — will that integrate with our CI to gate deploys if the QA evals regress?
[15:34] Priya: Yes — we have eval webhooks and a quality monitor: if a prompt-set regression is detected, you can block a rollout. We also provide small SDK helpers to run evals during CI.

[17:05] Jordan: One last technical dive — how do you handle KV cache eviction across model variants/eval? We sometimes get cache poisoning when models change tokenization.
[17:20] Priya: Good point — Redwood tracks KV cache keys by model artifact and sequence-length hash; when you pin a model version we avoid stale cache issues. If you roll to a new tokenization you should flush prefixes; we can automate this in rollout policies.

[19:00] Alex: Time wise we’re wrapping, but want to recap next steps and make sure we have owners.

Recap & Next steps:
- Alex to share sandbox key + console invite + quickstart repo link (action above)
- Priya to share CI examples and an integration test harness (action above)
- Kestrel to share workloads and SLOs for pilot (Jordan)
- Samir to send SOC2 and KMS preferences

[19:45] Jordan: Sounds good, thanks for pairing — the hands-on cleared a lot of questions. We’ll follow up on the SOC2 items and aim to run the pilot early Jan.
[19:55] Alex: Thanks everyone — I’ll email the packet and we’ll sync on the pilot schedule.

Note: transcript contains occasional mislabels and minor transcription errors (e.g., "kay-vee" for KV cache, "samm-el" for SAML). Also references to links and artifacts were shared in chat rather than pasted here.
